title: Pluto has an atmosphere, and looking back, New Horizons saw it glow as a ring

cover.alt: Pluto as a beige globe with darker brown patches and a large pale heart-shaped region, against black space.

body: Pluto is small and lies far out beyond Neptune, yet it holds on to a thin atmosphere, **mostly nitrogen** with a little methane and carbon monoxide. When New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015, it measured a surface pressure of about 1 pascal, roughly one hundred-thousandth of Earth’s. As the craft passed behind Pluto and looked back towards the Sun, sunlight shone through that air and lit it up as a thin glowing ring. Its images revealed a haze, blue in colour, that wraps the whole world and rises more than 200 km, in about 20 separate layers.

slides.alt: Animation built from New Horizons images: Pluto grows from a dot into a large beige globe with a pale heart-shaped patch, turns to a thin crescent as the view passes behind it, then becomes a dark disc outlined by a faint glowing ring, before a bright Sun appears beside a small dark moon.
slides.caption: Animation from real New Horizons images, July 2015, slowed 1.5×: Pluto looms up, the view slips behind it, and sunlight glows through its atmosphere as a ring. Then the Sun appears by Charon.

slides.prompt: Pluto’s surface pressure is about 1 pascal. How does that compare with the air pressure on Earth?
slides.detail: The pressure had roughly tripled between 1988 and 2015, and has since dropped, to about 0.91 pascals by 2020.

slides.heading: What Pluto’s air is made of, apart from nitrogen
slides.note: Nearly all the rest is nitrogen

slides.question: In 1988, how did astronomers prove from Earth that Pluto has an atmosphere?
options: A star faded slowly behind it
They saw clouds on its surface
Its colour changed with the seasons
slides.explanation: When Pluto passed in front of a star, the starlight dimmed gradually instead of cutting off at once, as it would behind a world with no air.
